title: Least generic formal singular height controls low-height excellence
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian normal Nagata domain over $\mathbf Q$ [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring, def-weil-pbc-normal-ring, def-weil-pbc-nagata-ring]. Let $0\ne x\in R$ be a nonunit, and suppose $R$ is $(x)$-adically complete [def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring], universally catenary, not quasi-excellent, with every quotient $R/K$ for a nonzero ideal $K$ quasi-excellent [def-exc-excellent-ring]. For each finite extension $L/\operatorname{Frac}R$, let $B_L$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $L$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. Assume that $B_L$ is finite as an $R$-module, normal, Nagata, universally catenary and $(x)$-adically complete, that $B_L/xB_L$ is quasi-excellent, and that the maximal-ideal completion $\widehat{(B_L)_{\mathfrak n}}$ is a normal local domain for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$ of $B_L$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime, def-weil-pbc-adic-completion].

For each such $L,\mathfrak n$, put $C_{L,\mathfrak n}=\varprojlim_j (B_L)_{\mathfrak n}/x^j(B_L)_{\mathfrak n}$. For a Noetherian ring $T$, write $\operatorname{Sing}(T)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}T:T_{\mathfrak p}\text{ is not regular local}\}$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-regular-scheme]. A minimal singular prime is a member of this set containing no strictly smaller member. Define
$$\mathcal S=\{(L,\mathfrak n,\mathfrak s):\mathfrak s\text{ is a minimal singular prime of }C_{L,\mathfrak n},\ \mathfrak s\cap B_L=(0)\}.$$
Height means $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=\dim T_{\mathfrak p}$, with Krull dimension as in [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Then every $C_{L,\mathfrak n}$ is a Noetherian normal local G-ring [def-weil-pbc-g-ring], and its singular locus is closed. The set $\mathcal S$ is nonempty. Its heights have a least value $h\in\mathbf N$ with $h\geq2$, attained by some triple in $\mathcal S$. Every $R_{\mathfrak p}$ with $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p\leq h$, and every $(B_L)_{\mathfrak q}$ with $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q\leq h$, is excellent.

source.place: Kurano–Shimomoto, Ideal-adic completion of quasi-excellent rings (after Gabber), Theorem 5.1, Step 2, (5.1)–(5.6) and Claim 5.2, printed pp.9–11; final finite-extension consequence printed p.13; obtained in sandbox sources/kurano40.pdf (bibliographic integration requested in report.md).

proof.text: Fix $L,\mathfrak n$, and abbreviate $B=B_L$, $A=B_{\mathfrak n}$, $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak nA$, $C=C_{L,\mathfrak n}$. A finite module algebra is finite type (its module generators also generate it as an algebra). Hence $B$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian], $A$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-noetherian], and $C$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-adic-completion-noetherian]. By [lem-weil-pbc-adic-complete-jacobson-radical], $x$ belongs to every maximal ideal of $B$, so $x\in\mathfrak m$. By [lem-weil-pbc-adic-completion-mod-ideal], $C$ is $xC$-adically complete and $C/xC=A/xA$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 2, (5.1) and preparation for (5.3), printed p.9

proof.text: The quotient $C/xC=A/xA$ is local and $xC$ is in the Jacobson radical by [lem-weil-pbc-adic-complete-jacobson-radical]. Thus $C$ is local, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak mC$, and $A\to C$ is local. For each $j\geq1$, exact completion of $0\to\mathfrak m^j\to A\to A/\mathfrak m^j\to0$, together with its finite-module tensor description, gives $C/\mathfrak m^jC\cong(A/\mathfrak m^j)^{\wedge(x)}=A/\mathfrak m^j$: the last completion stabilizes because $x^j\in\mathfrak m^j$. These isomorphisms are induced by $A\to C$, hence commute with all quotient transitions. Taking inverse limits identifies $\widehat C=\widehat A$, compatibly with the maps from $A$ and $C$. This is a short quotient calculation, not an extra completion theorem.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 2, sentence preceding (5.3), printed p.9; expanded using Stacks Tags 00MA (lemma-completion-tensor) and 00MB (lemma-completion-flat)

proof.text: By [lem-per-quasi-excellent-localization], $A/xA$ is quasi-excellent, since it is a localization of the assumed quasi-excellent ring $B/xB$. In particular it is a G-ring. Apply [lem-per-local-g-ring-adic-lifting] to the local complete pair $(C,xC)$ from steps 1–2: $C$ is a G-ring. Apply [lem-per-semilocal-g-ring-j2] to this local ring: it is quasi-excellent and therefore has closed singular locus. The map $C\to\widehat C=\widehat A$ is regular by [lem-weil-pbc-g-ring-completion-regular] and faithfully flat by [lem-weil-pbc-local-completion-faithfully-flat]. The target is a normal local domain by the assumption on the maximal-adic completion of $(B_L)_{\mathfrak n}$. Hence [lem-sfb-faithfully-flat-normal-ring-descent] makes $C$ normal; as a local normal ring it is a domain. This proves every assertion about each individual $C_{L,\mathfrak n}$.

We record why only generic formal fibres can fail. For primes $0\ne\mathfrak t\subseteq\mathfrak p$ of $R$, $R/\mathfrak t$ is quasi-excellent by hypothesis; its localization at $\mathfrak p/\mathfrak t$ is quasi-excellent by [lem-per-quasi-excellent-localization]. Its completion map is regular by [lem-weil-pbc-g-ring-completion-regular]. The generic fibre of that map is geometrically regular, and [lem-weil-pbc-formal-fibre-quotient-iso] identifies it with the fibre over $\mathfrak t$ of $R_{\mathfrak p}\to\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}$. Thus all nonzero-prime fibres of every such completion map are geometrically regular.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 2, opening paragraph and Claim 5.2, printed pp.9–10

proof.text: The quotient $R/xR$ is quasi-excellent since $xR\ne0$, and $xR$ is in the Jacobson radical by [lem-weil-pbc-adic-complete-jacobson-radical]. If $R$ were a G-ring, [lem-per-g-ring-quasi-excellent-closed-fibre] would make it quasi-excellent, contrary to hypothesis. By [lem-weil-pbc-g-ring-maximal-ideal-criterion], choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$ whose local completion map is not regular. It is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-local-completion-faithfully-flat], so step 4 shows its generic fibre is not geometrically regular. Put $K=\operatorname{Frac}R$. Since $K$ has characteristic zero, a finite purely inseparable extension has degree one (an element with a $p$-power in the base can occur nontrivially only in characteristic $p>0$). Thus geometric regularity over $K$ is ordinary regularity by [def-weil-pbc-g-ring]. Consequently $K\otimes_R\widehat{R_{\mathfrak n}}$ is not regular.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 2, opening paragraph and generic-fibre square, printed p.9; characteristic-zero specialization

proof.text: Use $L=K$, so normality of $R$ gives $B_K=R$, and put $C=C_{K,\mathfrak n}$. If $K\otimes_R C$ were regular, every local ring of $\widehat{R_{\mathfrak n}}$ at a prime over $(0)$ would be regular: the corresponding local ring of $C$ is regular, the local map is flat with regular closed fibre because $C\to\widehat C$ is regular (step 3), and [lem-weil-pbc-flat-over-regular-with-regular-fibre] applies. This contradicts step 5. Choose a singular prime of $C$ contracting to zero. Since $\operatorname{Sing}C$ is closed, write it as $V(J)$; [lem-weil-pbc-prime-contains-minimal-prime] supplies a prime minimal over $J$ below the chosen prime. Its contraction to $R$ is still zero, so it gives a member of $\mathcal S$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 2, definition of $S_L$ and (5.2), printed p.9

proof.text: Every prime in each Noetherian $C$ has finite natural height by [lem-trf-noetherian-prime-finite-height]. The nonempty set of these natural heights therefore has a least element $h$, realized by a triple. Each $C$ is normal by step 3, hence satisfies $(R_1)$ by [lem-weil-pbc-serre-criterion-normal]. By the definition of $(R_1)$ in [def-weil-pbc-serre-conditions-rk-sk], a singular prime cannot have height zero or one. Hence $h\geq2$.

Let $0\ne\mathfrak p\subset R$ have height at most $h$, choose a maximal $\mathfrak n\supseteq\mathfrak p$, and put $C=C_{K,\mathfrak n}$, $A=R_{\mathfrak p}$. The map $R_{\mathfrak n}\to C$ is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-completion-flat] and local by step 2, hence faithfully flat by [lem-pc-local-flat-faithful-flat-reflects-surjective]. Thus $\mathfrak pC$ is proper: by [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-surjective-spectrum] some prime of $C$ contracts to $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak n}$, and it contains $\mathfrak pC$. Choose $Q$ minimal over $\mathfrak pC$ using [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-prime-over-proper-ideal]. Its contraction to $R$ is exactly $\mathfrak p$: otherwise [lem-sc-flat-going-down] would produce a strictly smaller prime over $\mathfrak p$ containing $\mathfrak pC$. The induced map $\alpha:A\to C_Q$ is flat and local, and its closed fibre has dimension zero because $Q$ is minimal over $\mathfrak pC$. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-flat-height-formula] gives $\operatorname{ht}Q=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p\leq h$. No finite-type assumption on this completion map is used.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 2, Claim 5.2, (5.5)–(5.6), printed p.10; specialized to $L=K$

proof.text: Put $T=\widehat{C_Q}$. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-noetherian] and [lem-weil-pbc-adic-completion-noetherian], these local rings are Noetherian. The map $\widehat\alpha:\widehat A\to T$ is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-completion], and it is local since the compatible completion map carries the extended maximal ideal of $A$ into that of $C_Q$; the description of these maximal ideals is [lem-weil-pbc-local-completion-local-ring]. It is faithfully flat by [lem-pc-local-flat-faithful-flat-reflects-surjective]. Since $C$ is a G-ring, the map $C_Q\to T$ is regular by [def-weil-pbc-g-ring].

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 2, Claim 5.2, diagram with alpha, completed alpha and beta, printed p.10

proof.text: Write $\operatorname{Sing}C=V(J)$, and let $s_1,\ldots,s_r$ be the primes minimal over $J$ which are contained in $Q$; there are finitely many by [lem-sc-finite-minimal-primes-over-ideal]. For each $s_i\subsetneq Q$, strict inclusion and finite heights give $\operatorname{ht}s_i<\operatorname{ht}Q\leq h$. Its contraction to $R$ must be nonzero: otherwise $(K,\mathfrak n,s_i)\in\mathcal S$ contradicts minimality of $h$. If $s_i=Q$, its contraction is the nonzero ideal $\mathfrak p$. Choose $0\ne b_i\in s_i\cap R$ and put $b=\prod_i b_i$, with $b=1$ if $r=0$. This is nonzero since $R$ is a domain. This product is the explicit common element in all the surviving singular components.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 2, Claim 5.2, three cases for the singular ideal, printed pp.10–11

proof.text: We claim $T[1/b]$ is regular. For a prime $P\subset T$ not containing $b$, contract it to a prime $s\subseteq Q$ of $C$. If $C_s$ were singular, [lem-weil-pbc-prime-contains-minimal-prime] would give a minimal singular prime $s_i\subseteq s$; it appears in step 10, forcing $b\in P$, a contradiction. Thus $C_s$ is regular. The map $C_s\to T_P$ is flat local with regular closed fibre: it is obtained by localization from the regular map $C_Q\to T$ of step 9. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-flat-over-regular-with-regular-fibre] to obtain that $T_P$ is regular. Since localization preserves Noetherianity by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-noetherian], this proves the claim. This pointwise argument supplies explicitly the source's assertion that the singular ideal extends to a defining ideal of $\operatorname{Sing}T$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 2, Claim 5.2, regularity of $T[1/b]$, printed p.11

proof.text: Faithful flatness of $\widehat\alpha$ gives, by [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-surjective-spectrum], for every prime $P$ of $\widehat A$ avoiding $b$ a prime of $T$ over it, also avoiding $b$. The local map of the corresponding prime localizations is flat, and its target is regular by step 11. By [lem-weil-pbc-flat-under-regular], $\widehat A_P$ is regular. Localizing once more preserves regular local rings by [lem-weil-pbc-regular-local-localization]. Every prime of $K\otimes_R\widehat A$ avoids the nonzero $b$, so this generic fibre is regular. As in step 5, characteristic zero makes it geometrically regular. Together with step 4 and flatness of the completion map [lem-weil-pbc-local-completion-faithfully-flat], every fibre of $A\to\widehat A$ is geometrically regular; this map is regular.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 2, end of Claim 5.2, printed p.11

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-g-ring-maximal-ideal-criterion], the local ring $A=R_{\mathfrak p}$ is a G-ring, since its only maximal-local completion map is the regular map of step 12. Then [lem-per-semilocal-g-ring-j2] makes $A$ quasi-excellent. It is universally catenary by the definition in [def-exc-excellent-ring]: a finite type $R_{\mathfrak p}$-algebra is the localization, at $R\setminus\mathfrak p$, of a finite type $R$-algebra (choose finitely many algebra generators and clear denominators in finitely many defining equations, possible since $R$ is Noetherian). Between two primes surviving a localization every intermediate prime also survives, so the saturated chains and their lengths agree. Universal catenarity of $R$ therefore supplies it for $A$. Thus $A$ is excellent. At $\mathfrak p=0$, the local ring is the field $K$, excellent by [lem-exc-fields-excellent].

Finally fix $L$ and $\mathfrak q\subset B_L$ of height at most $h$, and put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$. Apply [lem-exc-dimension-formula-universally-catenary-finite-type-domain] to the finite extension of domains $R\subset B_L$: its fraction field extension and its residue field extension at $\mathfrak q$ are algebraic, so both transcendence degrees are zero and $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q\leq h$. Hence $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is excellent by step 13. The algebra $B_L\otimes_R R_{\mathfrak p}$ is finite, hence finite type over this ring, and $(B_L)_{\mathfrak q}$ is its localization. Apply [lem-exc-finite-type-localization-excellent] to obtain excellence of $(B_L)_{\mathfrak q}$. This includes height zero, where the localizations are fields.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 2, finite-extension consequence following Claim 5.4, printed p.13
